            "Gluing separate points together is also strictly forbidden.",
            "These rules preserve the object's fundamental structure."
        ]

        WHITE_LABEL = "#FFFFFF"
        RED_X = "#FF0000"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = "#FFFF00"

        self.lecture[0].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        
        # Create an orange blob shape (using a rounded rectangle for 'dough' feel)
        blob = RoundedRectangle(corner_radius=1, height=2, width=2, fill_color=ORANGE_BLOB, fill_opacity=1, stroke_width=0)
        # Resolved Issue 42: blob area adjusted to B2-D5 to prevent overlap with labels
        self.place_in_area(blob, "B2", "D5", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        label = Text("Play-dough", font_size=20, color=WHITE_LABEL)
        # Resolved Issue 41: label moved to area E2-E4 and scaled down to avoid cut-off
        self.place_in_area(label, 'E2', 'E4', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(blob), Write(label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        
        # Stretch horizontal
        self.play(blob.animate.stretch(2.5, 0), run_time=1)
        self.play(blob.animate.stretch(1/2.5, 0), run_time=1)
        
        # Squish vertical
        self.play(blob.animate.stretch(0.3, 1), run_time=1)
        self.play(blob.animate.stretch(1/0.3, 1), run_time=1)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)

        # Puncture hole
        # Centers hole on the current blob position
        hole = Circle(radius=0.4, color=BLACK, fill_opacity=1).move_to(blob.get_center())
        cross_mark = Cross(blob, stroke_color=RED_X, stroke_width=10)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(hole))
        self.play(Create(cross_mark))
        self.wait(1)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(cross_mark), FadeOut(hole))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===

        self.lecture[3].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)

        # Cut into two pieces
        blob_left = RoundedRectangle(corner_radius=0.5, height=2, width=0.9, fill_color=ORANGE_BLOB, fill_opacity=1, stroke_width=0)
        blob_right = RoundedRectangle(corner_radius=0.5, height=2, width=0.9, fill_color=ORANGE_BLOB, fill_opacity=1, stroke_width=0)
        
        blob_left.move_to(blob.get_center() + LEFT*0.55)
        blob_right.move_to(blob.get_center() + RIGHT*0.55)
        
        self.remove(blob)
        self.add(blob_left, blob_right)
        
        cross_mark_2 = Cross(VGroup(blob_left, blob_right), stroke_color=RED_X, stroke_width=10)
        
        self.play(blob_left.animate.shift(LEFT*0.5), blob_right.animate.shift(RIGHT*0.5))
        self.play(Create(cross_mark_2))
        self.wait(1)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(cross_mark_2), FadeOut(blob_left), FadeOut(blob_right))
        self.add(blob)
        self.play(FadeIn(blob))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)

        # Pulse to show structure preserved
        self.play(blob.animate.scale(1.1), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(blob.animate.scale(1/1.1), run_time=0.5)
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: The Mug and the Donut Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the core concept: Topology is 'Rubber Sheet Geometry.' It focuses on properties that remain unchanged when an object is stretched or deformed without being torn or glued.
sections.example: An animation showing a 3D ceramic coffee mug smoothly morphing into a glazed donut (torus) to show they are 'topologically equivalent'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Euclidean vs. Topological Thinking
sections.content: Contrast traditional geometry (where distance and angles matter) with topology (where only connectivity matters). Explain that in topology, a circle and a square are the same thing.
sections.example: A visual comparison of a rigid wooden square (Euclidean) vs. a flexible rubber band (Topological) that can be pulled into various shapes while retaining its 'loopiness'.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Homeomorphism
sections.content: Define the 'allowed' moves: bending, stretching, and squishing. Define the 'forbidden' moves: cutting, puncturing, or gluing points together.
sections.example: A character made of play-dough. We can stretch his arms long (allowed), but we cannot poke a new hole through his stomach or tear his head off (forbidden).

sections.title: Topological Invariants: Euler Characteristic
sections.content: Introduce the formula Chi (χ) = V - E + F (Vertices minus Edges plus Faces). Explain that this number stays constant for all shapes that can be deformed into a sphere.
sections.example: A 3D animation showing a cube (8V, 12E, 6F) inflating into a sphere. The calculation 8 - 12 + 6 = 2 is displayed on screen, showing χ=2.

sections.title: Classification by Genus (Holes)
sections.content: Introduce 'Genus' (g) as a way to categorize shapes. Genus is essentially the number of 'holes' in a surface. This is a primary way topologists distinguish objects.
sections.example: A sorting machine graphic: A sphere (g=0) goes in one bin; a wedding ring and a straw (g=1) go in another; a pretzel (g=3) goes in a third.

sections.title: Topology in Connectivity: Graphs
sections.content: Shift from surfaces to networks. Explain that the physical length of a path doesn't matter as much as how the nodes are connected.
sections.example: The London Underground map (a topological map) vs. a satellite view of London. Show how the map simplifies the 'messy' real world into clear, functional nodes.

sections.title: Modern Applications
sections.content: Show how topology applies to complex systems like DNA folding, circuit design, and data analysis (TDA).
sections.example: A stylized animation of a DNA strand knotting and unknotting to show how nature solves topological tangles to replicate life.

sections.title: Summary: The Essence of Shape
sections.content: Recap: Topology looks past the details of size and scale to find the fundamental structure of an object or space.
sections.example: A fast-motion montage of all the previous shapes (mug, donut, rubber band, cube) collapsing into their core topological categories (Genus 0, 1, etc.).

However, you cannot tear or puncture the material.
Gluing separate points together is also strictly forbidden.
These rules preserve the object's fundamental structure.
animations: Create an orange blob shape representing play-dough (#FFA500). Label: 'Play-dough' (#FFFFFF).
Stretch the blob horizontally to 3x its width, then back to normal.
Squish the blob into a thin vertical line, then back to normal.
A red 'X' (#FF0000) appears as a hole is punched through the blob, which then resets.
A red 'X' (#FF0000) appears as the blob is cut into two pieces, which then resets.

storyboard.title: Topological Invariants: Euler Characteristic
lecture_lines: Topological invariants are properties that never change.
The Euler Characteristic uses vertices, edges, and faces.
For any sphere-like object, the result is always two.
This formula reveals a shape's hidden mathematical constant.
Invariants help us distinguish between different topological spaces.
animations: Render a blue cube (#00BFFF). Label 'V=8, E=12, F=6' (#FFFFFF) next to it.
Calculate 8 - 12 + 6 and display the result 'Chi = 2' (#00FF00) in the center.
Morph the cube into a sphere (#00BFFF) while keeping the text 'Chi = 2' static.
Show a tetrahedron (#00BFFF) and display its calculation: '4 - 6 + 4 = 2' (#00FF00).
Highlight both '2' results with a glowing white box (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Classification by Genus (Holes)
lecture_lines: Genus counts the number of holes in a surface.
Spheres have genus zero; rings have genus one.
More complex objects have even higher genus values.
animations: Display three boxes at the bottom labeled 'Genus 0', 'Genus 1', and 'Genus 2+' (#FFFFFF).
A sphere (#FFFFFF) moves into 'Genus 0'. A ring [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/ring.svg] moves into 'Genus 1'.
A double-holed button [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/button.svg] moves into 'Genus 2+'.

storyboard.title: Topology in Connectivity: Graphs
lecture_lines: Topology also applies to connections in a network.
Map distances matter less than how nodes are linked.
The London Underground map illustrates this topological simplicity.
animations: Show a network of nodes (#FFFFFF) connected by curved, varied-length lines (#708090).
Straighten and color the lines (blue, red, green) to resemble a subway map (#1E90FF) accompanied by the [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/subway.svg] icon.
Pulse the nodes in yellow (#FFFF00) to show connectivity is preserved.

storyboard.title: Modern Applications
lecture_lines: Topology helps scientists understand complex DNA knotting.
It optimizes data analysis and electronic circuit design.
These principles solve real-world problems through shape analysis.
animations: Show two intertwined green loops representing a DNA knot (#00FA9A) [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/dna.svg].
Animate the loops sliding through each other (topological unknotting) to form two separate circles.
Label the final circles 'Unknotted' (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Summary: The Essence of Shape
lecture_lines: Topology finds the essence of shape beyond measurements.
It categorizes the universe through connectivity and holes.
This "rubber geometry" reveals the core of mathematical structure.
animations: Show a sphere, a cube, and a donut [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/donut.svg] on screen.
Morph the sphere and cube into simple points (#FFFFFF), and the donut [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/donut.svg] into a circle (#FFFFFF).
Display text 'The Science of Continuity' (#00FF00) in large font.
